content: The global HIV/AIDS epidemic has persisted for over 30 years, with infection rates remaining alarmingly high. More than 2.7 million people are newly infected with HIV each year, highlighting the urgent need for more effective prevention strategies. Oral antiretroviral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) has emerged as a potential tool to prevent HIV transmission in individuals at high risk of infection. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of oral antiretroviral chemoprophylaxis in preventing HIV infection among HIV-uninfected individuals who are at high risk. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in April 2012 across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and EMBASE. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and ClinicalTrials.gov. The review included randomized controlled trials that evaluated the use of any antiretroviral agent or combination of agents for HIV prevention in high-risk populations. Data on outcomes, intervention details, and study characteristics were extracted independently by two authors using a standardized form. The measure of effect was expressed as relative risk (RR) with a 95% confidence interval (CI). A total of 12 randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria for this review. Of these, six trials were ongoing, four had been completed, and two were terminated early. Data from six studies involving 9,849 participants were analyzed. The trials investigated the following interventions: daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) combined with emtricitabine (FTC) versus placebo, TDF alone versus placebo, and daily TDF-FTC versus intermittent TDF-FTC. One trial included three study arms: TDF, TDF-FTC, and placebo. The studies were conducted among various high-risk groups, including HIV-uninfected men who have sex with men, serodiscordant couples (where one partner is HIV-positive and the other is HIV-negative), and other high-risk men and women. The results from four trials comparing TDF-FTC to placebo demonstrated a significant reduction in the risk of acquiring HIV infection, with a relative risk of 0.49 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.85) among 8,918 participants. Similarly, studies comparing TDF alone to placebo showed a substantial reduction in HIV acquisition risk, with a relative risk of 0.33 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.55) among 4,027 participants. Importantly, there were no significant differences in the incidence of adverse events between the intervention and control groups across all studies. Additionally, adherence to the intervention and sexual behaviors were comparable between the groups. The findings of this review indicate that pre-exposure prophylaxis using TDF alone or in combination with FTC effectively reduces the risk of HIV acquisition in high-risk populations. This includes individuals in serodiscordant relationships, men who have sex with men, and other high-risk men and women.
